input.title: Auth on an unsigned-header document does not resist an adversary, so an enforceable policy needs a signed header — ideally with INITIALIZE_AUTH in the create batch

input.description: With no creator the genesis is open: anyone can run INITIALIZE_AUTH first, or backdate one that re-evaluates the whole history under a policy of their choosing. Migrated documents all lack a creator.

Extracted from apps/academy/docs/academy/05-Lookup/00-Cookbook.md at v6.2.2-dev.74 — Document ACL / Group Principals: signer context attached by hand vs ReactorClient.withSigner

input.content:
A document's policy begins with `INITIALIZE_AUTH`, and its creator is whoever signed the header. An **unsigned-header document has no creator**, so its genesis is open: anyone can run `INITIALIZE_AUTH` first, and — because judgment is positional — anyone can *backdate* one that retroactively re-evaluates the whole history under a policy of their choosing. The spec states it flatly: auth on such a document does not resist an adversary.

The rule that follows: a document that wants an enforceable policy is **created with a signed header**, ideally with `INITIALIZE_AUTH` in its create batch so no window exists between existence and policy. The recipes attach unsigned `action.context.signer` by hand only to play several callers from one process; in production the `ReactorClient` populates and signs it via `.withSigner(...)` (the `audit-trail` recipe shows a real `RenownCryptoSigner`).

The same fact shapes the migration of the host's permission tables (stage 9): no existing document has a signed header, so a genesis binds no creator whoever signs it, and every migrated policy must therefore carry an explicit `execute`-on-`auth` grant naming the table's owner — or be refused as born locked out. A document with no owner is refused and reported rather than given an administrator its access list never mentioned.
